config.title: useFetch

intro.title: useFetch
intro.body: In this lesson you will build a reusable `useFetch` hook that calls an API and tracks **data**, **loading**, and **error**. First you will meet **TypeScript generics**: the hook cannot know the JSON shape in advance, so you will name that unknown type **`T`** and describe the hook's return value with **`FetchResponse<T>`** — where **`data`** is **`T | null`**. Then you wire **`useState`**, **`useEffect`**, and **`fetch`**, and render loading state in a small **App** demo.
intro.usecase: The useFetch pattern is essential for any React application that displays dynamic data from an API. Centralizing fetch + loading + error in a hook keeps components small and reusable across dashboards, product lists, and profile screens.

objectives: Define a generic interface for async hook results: data as T | null, plus loading and error fields
Declare useFetch<T>(url) with a return type tied to that interface
Implement state and an async fetch helper inside the hook
Trigger fetches when the URL changes using useEffect
Return live state from the hook and consume it in a component with conditional UI

steps.title: Import React, useState, and useEffect
steps.instruction: Import **React** (default import), and **useState** and **useEffect** (named imports), from `'react'`.
steps.hint: Correct pattern: `import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';` — not `{ React, useState }` (React is usually the default import).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: default + named hooks
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The file can use JSX (React) plus both hooks.
successCriteria: React, useState, and useEffect are imported from 'react' with valid syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You need the default React import and two named hooks: useState and useEffect.

steps.title: Define FetchResponse<T> (generic result shape)
steps.instruction: Below the import, define a TypeScript interface **`FetchResponse<T>`** with three properties: **`data`** typed as **`T | null`**, **`loading`** as **`boolean`**, and **`error`** as **`string | null`**. The **`<T>`** is a **type parameter**: it stands for “whatever JSON shape this fetch will return” — you will plug in a concrete type (or let inference help) when you call the hook later.
steps.hint: Syntax: `interface FetchResponse<T> { ... }`. **`T`** must appear in angle brackets on the interface name so TypeScript knows `data` can use `T`. This is not the browser's `Response` class from `fetch` — it's *your* name for “what the hook returns.”
steps.expectedOutcome: You have a reusable, generic description of the hook's return shape.
successCriteria: An interface FetchResponse<T> declares data (T | null), loading (boolean), and error (string | null).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check: `interface FetchResponse<T>`, `data` uses `T | null`, and both `loading` and `error` use the right types.
steps.feedbackWrong: Define `interface FetchResponse<T> { ... }` with the three fields and types above. Without `<T>` on the interface, `T` in `data` is unknown to the compiler.

steps.title: Declare useFetch<T> with the correct return type
steps.instruction: Declare a function **`useFetch`** that is generic in **`T`**, takes one parameter **`url`** of type **`string`**, and is annotated to return **`FetchResponse<T>`**. For this step only, the body may return a **stub object**: `{ data: null, loading: false, error: null }` — you will replace the placeholder with real state in the following steps.
steps.hint: Signature shape: `function useFetch<T>(url: string): FetchResponse<T> { ... }`. The `<T>` on **`useFetch`** ties the caller's type argument to **`FetchResponse<T>`**.
steps.expectedOutcome: The hook exists and type-checks: URL in, FetchResponse<T> out.
successCriteria: useFetch is generic, takes url: string, return type is FetchResponse<T>, stub return matches the three fields.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Ensure both **`useFetch`** and **`FetchResponse`** use the same **`<T>`** and the return object includes data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add `function useFetch<T>(url: string): FetchResponse<T>` and return `{ data: null, loading: false, error: null }` for now.

steps.title: Initialize data, loading, and error with useState
steps.instruction: Inside **`useFetch`**, replace the hard-coded stub values by initializing three pieces of state: **`data`** with **`useState<T | null>(null)`**, **`loading`** with **`useState<boolean>(false)`** (or `useState(false)`), and **`error`** with **`useState<string | null>(null)`**. Keep returning the stub object for one more step, or return `{ data, loading, error }` if you already prefer — the next steps will focus on fetching.
steps.hint: You need `setData`, `setLoading`, and `setError` from destructuring. Generic on data: `useState<T | null>(null)`.
steps.expectedOutcome: Hook holds typed state for the three fields.
successCriteria: Three useState calls exist with types T | null, boolean, and string | null (or equivalent inference) for data, loading, error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure `data` uses `T | null` in useState's generic.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add useState for data (typed with T), loading, and error inside useFetch.

steps.title: Add the fetchData async helper
steps.instruction: Inside **`useFetch`**, define an **`async`** function **`fetchData`** that accepts a **`string`** URL, calls **`fetch(url)`**, reads JSON with **`.json()`**, and uses your setters to update **`data`**, **`loading`**, and **`error`** (start loading true, clear error; on success set data and loading false; on failure set error message and loading false). You can use **`try` / `catch`**.
steps.hint: Pattern: set loading true → try { const res = await fetch(u); const json = await res.json(); setData(json); } catch (e) { setError(...); } finally { setLoading(false); }
steps.expectedOutcome: Fetch logic is encapsulated in one async helper using setters.
successCriteria: An async fetchData(url) uses fetch, await, and updates the three state fields appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Ensure you await fetch and response.json(), and toggle loading around the attempt.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add `async function fetchData(…)` inside the hook with fetch + try/catch + setters.

steps.title: Run fetch when the URL changes (useEffect)
steps.instruction: Add **`useEffect`** that calls **`fetchData(url)`** when **`url`** changes. Put **`url`** in the dependency array: **`[url]`**.
steps.hint: useEffect(() => { fetchData(url); }, [url]); — eslint rules of hooks: call useEffect at top level of the hook, not inside fetchData.
steps.expectedOutcome: Changing `url` from a parent re-runs the request.
successCriteria: useEffect calls fetchData with the hook's url and lists url in the dependency array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Include [url] as the second argument to useEffect.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add useEffect that invokes fetchData(url) and depends on [url].

steps.title: Return the live state object
steps.instruction: Ensure **`return { data, loading, error }`** uses your **state variables** (not fresh literals). If you already do, this step is a quick check.
steps.hint: Return must match `FetchResponse<T>`: same three keys, variables not `null`/`false` literals unless you intentionally reset.
steps.expectedOutcome: Consumers of the hook see updated state after fetch completes.
successCriteria: Return statement uses the data, loading, and error state bindings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Replace any `{ data: null, ... }` stub with `{ data, loading, error }`.
steps.feedbackWrong: Return the three state variables by name: `{ data, loading, error }`.

steps.title: Add the App component shell
steps.instruction: Below the hook, define a function component **`App`** that returns a **`div`** containing an **`h1`** (e.g. "useFetch demo"). Export **`App`** as default at the bottom of the file.
steps.expectedOutcome: Preview can mount a default export component.
successCriteria: App exists, returns JSX with div + h1, default export App.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Add `export default App;` at the end.
steps.feedbackWrong: Define `function App()` with JSX and export it as default.

steps.title: Call useFetch with a type argument and sample URL
steps.instruction: Inside **`App`**, call **`useFetch`** with a **type argument** for the JSONPlaceholder todo shape and pass the URL **`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1`**. Destructure **`data`**, **`loading`**, and **`error`**. Example type (you can paste inline): `{ userId: number; id: number; title: string; completed: boolean }`.
steps.hint: `const { data, loading, error } = useFetch<{ userId: number; id: number; title: string; completed: boolean }>("https://...");`
steps.analogousExample:
type Todo = { userId: number; id: number; title: string; completed: boolean };
const { data, loading } = useFetch<Todo>(url);
steps.expectedOutcome: App receives typed data from the hook for the sample endpoint.
successCriteria: useFetch is called with a generic type and the jsonplaceholder URL; data, loading, and error are destructured.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Add `<{ ... }>` between useFetch and the parenthesis with the URL string.
steps.feedbackWrong: Call `useFetch<YourTodoShape>('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1')` at the top of App and destructure all three fields.

steps.feedbackCorrect: You're done — solid work tying generics to a real fetch hook.
